mainTopic: How a city's boundaries are set for תחום שבת: the קרפף, bow-shaped cities, wall remnants, structures near a city, and hut settlements.
overview: The amud opens by explaining why רב הונא had to say 'a קרפף for each side' twice, once for a split city and once for two neighboring cities. The answer is צריכא: each case has its own reason. Next, the גמרא asks how deep a bow-shaped city may curve before we stop drawing a straight bowstring line, and אביי sides with the view that even more than 2,000 אמות is fine. The גמרא then defines the משנה's גדודיות as three walls without a roof. It asks about two walls with a roof and tries to answer from a ברייתא listing what does and does not count as part of a city, but the proof is rejected. Two items from that list, a house on the sea and a cave, are then explained. רב הונא rules that hut-dwellers measure their תחום from their own doors. רבא defends this against a challenge from the desert camp, and רב אשי sets a minimum for a hut settlement to count as fixed. An אגדה section describes the hard life of hut-dwellers and gives two reasons for it. The amud ends with רב הונא's teaching about cities without vegetables and the start of a ברייתא that challenges it; that challenge continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The משנה: giving a city a קרפף
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה. רבי מאיר says every city gets a קרפף added to its edge. חכמים say a קרפף is only used for the space between two cities.
steps.simpleTranslation: We add a קרפף to a city. These are the words of רבי מאיר. The חכמים say: the measure of a קרפף was only given for the space between two cities.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings in the משנה as background. It is setting up the next step, where a מחלוקת among אמוראים will be connected to רב הונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי מאיר, every city gets an extra strip of about 70 אמות before we start measuring its תחום שבת. According to חכמים, that measure only matters when we ask whether two cities are close enough to count as one. The next step builds on the חכמים's view.

keyTerms.meaning: An enclosed open area, about 70⅔ אמות. Here it is used as a fixed measure of space.
The 2,000-אמה limit for walking outside a city on שבת.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think חכמים deny the קרפף measure altogether. They only limit where it is used: for the gap between two cities, not as an automatic extra strip for every city.

phrases.english: One gives a karpef to the city,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And the Sages say:
They did not speak of a karpef
except between two cities.

steps.triggerLanguage: נוֹתְנִין קַרְפֵּף לָעִיר, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings in the משנה as the foundation for a challenge to רב הונא's earlier ruling about a split city.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: every city gets a קרפף. חכמים: the קרפף measure only applies to the space between two cities.

steps.title: רב הונא already said 'a קרפף for each'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites a מחלוקת. רב הונא says each of the two cities gets its own קרפף, while חייא בר רב says they share one. So רב הונא already stated this rule. Why did he repeat it for the split city?
steps.simpleTranslation: And it was stated: רב הונא said, a קרפף for this city and a קרפף for that city. חייא בר רב said, we give only one קרפף for both of them. (So רב הונא already taught this!)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רב הונא already said the 'two קרפפים' rule about two neighboring cities. That makes his ruling about the split city seem unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב הונא, two cities count as one if the gap between them is less than two קרפפים (about 141 אמות). According to חייא בר רב, the gap must be less than one קרפף. Since רב הונא's view on two cities matches what he said about the split city, the גמרא asks, without spelling it out: why say it twice?

keyTerms.meaning: And it was stated (a ruling of the אמוראים).

steps.confusionAlert: There is no question word here. The exclamation at the end is the challenge itself: 'רב הונא already said this!' The point is that his earlier ruling repeats this one.

phrases.english: And it was stated:
Rav Huna said:
A karpef for this one and a karpef for that one.
And Chiyya bar Rav said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין נוֹתְנִין אֶלָּא קַרְפֵּף אֶחָד לִשְׁנֵיהֶם!
phrases.english: One gives only one karpef for the two of them!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיתְּמַר, רַב הוּנָא אָמַר: קַרְפֵּף לָזוֹ וְקַרְפֵּף לָזוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the חכמים's view in the משנה and shows that רב הונא already ruled 'two קרפפים' in the two-city case.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's earlier ruling that each section of a split city gets its own קרפף.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same rule already appears in רב הונא's statement about two cities, so stating it again seems pointless.

steps.title: First reason both rulings are needed: the split city was once permitted
steps.stepSummary: If רב הונא had only ruled on the split city, we would say it gets two קרפפים because it started out as one permitted city. Two separate cities would get no such leniency.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is necessary. Had he taught us only here (the split city), we would say that is because it had a permitted status from the start. But there (two separate cities), we would say no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with צריכא: both statements are needed. It starts by explaining why the split-city ruling alone would not have taught us the two-city ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A city that split was originally one unit, so we might be lenient and treat it generously. Two cities that were always separate never had that status. So from the split city alone, we might have given them only one קרפף.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary (both statements are needed).
He taught us / let us hear.
A permitted status from the very start.

phrases.english: It is necessary,
for had he taught us only here,

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דַּהֲוָה לֵיהּ צַד הֶיתֵּר מֵעִיקָּרָא.
phrases.english: one would say it is because it had an aspect of permissibility from the outset.
But there, I would say not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the challenge of repetition.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: each case has its own distinct reason.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the split city alone, we would think two separate cities get only one קרפף.
steps.terutzMaskana: The two-city ruling is needed to teach that they also get two קרפפים.

steps.title: Second reason both rulings are needed: two cities crowd each other
steps.stepSummary: If רב הונא had only ruled on two cities, we would say they get two קרפפים because sharing one would be too crowded. Inside a split city it is not crowded, so the split-city ruling is also needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And had he taught us only there (two cities), we would say that is because their use of the space would be crowded. But here (the split city), where their use is not crowded, we would say no. Therefore both are necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the צריכא by showing why the two-city ruling alone would not have taught us the split-city ruling. It concludes that both statements were needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two full cities sharing one קרפף would crowd each other, so giving each one its own makes sense. The empty area inside a split city was never used heavily, so one קרפף might seem enough there. That is why רב הונא had to say both.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב הונא, a קרפף is given to each side in both cases. Each case has its own reason: the split city was once permitted, and two cities would be crowded with only one. Neither case teaches the other, so both statements are needed (צריכא).
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic צריכותא pattern. Each case has its own source of leniency, and each reason applies to only one case. So the הלכה must be stated in both places.

phrases.english: And had he taught us only there,
one would say it is because their use would be cramped,
but here, where their use is not cramped,
I would say not. Therefore it is necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the second half of the צריכא begun in the previous step.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: each case has its own distinct reason.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the two-city case alone, we would think a split city gets only one קרפף, since its space is not crowded.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both rulings are necessary, so רב הונא's statement is not repetitive.

steps.title: How far can the curve be from the bowstring?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how much distance is allowed between the imaginary bowstring and the curve of a bow-shaped city.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how much distance may there be between the bowstring and the bow?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a measuring question about a city shaped like a bow (קשת). It wants to know the largest gap between the curve and the imaginary straight line across its two ends.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a bow-shaped city, we draw an imaginary straight line (יתר, the bowstring) between the two ends and measure תחום שבת from that line. The question is whether this works no matter how deep the curve is, or only up to a certain distance.

keyTerms.meaning: Bowstring: the imaginary straight line drawn between the two ends of a curved city
Bow: a city whose houses curve like a bow
And how much may it be?

phrases.english: And how much may there be
between the bowstring and the bow?
phrases.notes: The distance from the imaginary straight line to the deepest point of the curve

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new measuring question about a bow-shaped city.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The largest gap allowed between the bowstring line and the curve of the city.

steps.title: Father and son disagree: 2,000 אמות or even more
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא says the gap may be up to 2,000 אמות. His son רבא says it may be even more than 2,000.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said: up to 2,000 אמות. רבא, son of רבה בר רב הונא, said: even more than 2,000 אמות.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים, a father and his son, answer the question differently. One sets a limit of 2,000 אמות, and the other says there is no such limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר רב הונא holds that we only draw the bowstring if the curve is within 2,000 אמות of it, the size of a תחום שבת. His son רבא holds that we draw the bowstring even when the curve is deeper than 2,000 אמות.

keyTerms.meaning: Two thousand אמות, the standard size of a תחום שבת

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the names. רבה בר רב הונא is the father (2,000 limit). רבא בריה דרבה בר רב הונא is his son (even more than 2,000). This רבא is not the famous רבא who argues with אביי.

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said:
Two thousand cubits.

phrases.aramaic: רָבָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rava, son of Rabba bar Rav Huna, said:
Even more than two thousand cubits.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר אַלְפַּיִם אַמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 5 with a disagreement.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One view says 2,000 אמות is the limit. The other says there is no limit, even beyond 2,000.

steps.title: אביי sides with the son: you could walk through the houses anyway
steps.stepSummary: אביי says logic supports רבא, because a person could reach the bowstring line anyway by walking along the houses of the city.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: It makes sense to follow רבא son of רבה בר רב הונא, because if a person wants, he can go back and walk there by way of the houses.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a logical reason to side with the son, רבא, who allows even more than 2,000 אמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The houses along the curve are all part of the city, so a person can walk along them to the ends of the bow and then along the bowstring line. Since he can reach that line anyway, treating the empty space inside the curve as part of the city gives him nothing new. So no 2,000-אמה limit is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: It stands to reason, it makes sense logically
By way of the houses, walking through the built-up city

steps.whatToRemember: For a bow-shaped city, אביי sides with רבא: we draw the straight bowstring line even if the curve is more than 2,000 אמות deep, since one can walk through the houses anyway.

phrases.english: Abaye said:

phrases.aramaic: כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרָבָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא מִסְתַּבְּרָא,
phrases.english: It stands to reason in accordance with Rava, son of Rabba bar Rav Huna,
since if he wants,
he can go back and come by way of the houses.
phrases.notes: He walks along the houses to the ends of the bow, then along the bowstring line

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרָבָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא מִסְתַּבְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides between the two opinions of step 6 using logic.
steps.raayaObject: The view of רבא son of רבה בר רב הונא, which allows even more than 2,000 אמות.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Logic: a person can reach the bowstring line anyway by walking along the houses.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The bowstring is drawn even when the curve is deeper than 2,000 אמות.

steps.title: The משנה's line about wall remnants
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: if there were גדודיות ten טפחים high, they count as part of the city.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: If there were גדודיות ten טפחים high, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה so it can explain it. This sets up the next step, which asks what the word means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that standing wall remnants at the edge of a city, ten טפחים tall, are treated as part of the city. That pushes out the point from which we measure the תחום. The word גדודיות is unclear, so the גמרא is about to define it.

keyTerms.meaning: Wall remnants: leftover standing walls of a structure
Ten handbreadths, the standard minimum height of a halachic wall
Etc.: the quote continues in the משנה

phrases.english: If there were remnants of walls there
ten handbreadths high, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיוּ שָׁם גְּדוּדִיּוֹת גְּבוֹהוֹת עֲשָׂרָה טְפָחִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the bow-shaped city and goes back to another phrase in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wall remnants ten טפחים high at the edge of a city count as part of the city.

steps.title: What are גדודיות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exactly the משנה means by גדודיות.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are גדודיות?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the definition of the unclear word in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We need to know what kind of structure this is, such as how many walls and whether it has a roof, to know when it counts as part of the city.

phrases.english: What are remnants?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the term just quoted.

steps.title: רב יהודה: three walls with no roof
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה defines גדודיות as three walls without a roof.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: three walls that have no roof over them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question. גדודיות are three walls standing with no roof on top.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This structure is not a full house, yet three walls are enough for it to count as part of the city. This raises the next question: what about fewer walls with a roof?

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
Three partitions
that do not have a roof over them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה שָׁלֹשׁ מְחִיצּוֹת שֶׁאֵין עֲלֵיהֶן תִּקְרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: גדודיות are three walls with no roof.

steps.title: What about two walls with a roof?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether two walls with a roof on top also count as part of the city.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: two walls with a roof over them, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new question, an איבעיא. Three walls without a roof count, but what about only two walls that have a roof?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case has one wall fewer than רב יהודה's case but adds a roof. The question is whether the roof makes up for the missing wall, so the structure still counts as part of the city.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among them: an open question the גמרא tries to resolve

phrases.english: A dilemma was raised before them:
Two partitions
that have a roof over them, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ שְׁתֵּי מְחִיצּוֹת וְיֵשׁ עֲלֵיהֶן תִּקְרָה מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רב יהודה's definition by asking about a different combination of walls and roof.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether two walls with a roof count as part of the city like three walls without a roof.

steps.title: A list of structures counted as part of the city
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא listing structures that count as part of the city, as the start of a proof for the איבעיא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: These count as part of the city: a monument over a grave that is 4 by 4 אמות; a bridge or grave that has a living space; a synagogue with a living space for the attendant; an idolatrous temple with a living space for its priests; stables and storehouses in the fields that have a living space; small watchtowers within it; and a house on the sea. All of these count as part of the city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says 'come and hear' and quotes a ברייתא, a long list of structures that count as part of the city. This is setup only. The ברייתא goes on with a second list in the next step, and in step 14 the גמרא points to one item from that second list to try to answer the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each item counts because it is a real structure or has a living space in it. This first list is only background. The proof the גמרא will try to draw, in step 14, comes from the second list of things that are NOT included (step 13).

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: introduces a source brought as proof
Are included with it: counted as part of the city when measuring the תחום
A monument built over a grave
A living space, a place where someone lives

steps.confusionAlert: The proof is not finished here. The list is only quoted here. The גמרא draws its conclusion from it in the next lines.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
These are included with it (the city):
a monument that has
four cubits by four cubits,
and the bridge and the grave
that have a living space in them,
and a synagogue that has
a living space for the attendant,
and an idolatrous temple that has
a living space for the priests,
and the stables and storehouses in the fields
that have a living space in them,
and the small watchtowers within it,
and the house in the sea
these are all included with it (the city).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins an attempt to answer the איבעיא of step 11 from a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: The question of whether two walls with a roof count as part of the city.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא listing structures that are included in the city's boundaries. The inference from it comes next.

steps.title: The second half of the ברייתא: structures that are not part of the city
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא lists structures near a city that are NOT included in its boundaries. Most are buildings nobody lives in. One of them, the נפש breached on two sides, will be used in the next step as a proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: And these are not included with the city: a tomb-monument breached on two opposite sides, from one side through to the other; a bridge and a grave with no living quarters; a synagogue with no living quarters for the caretaker; an idol temple with no living quarters for its priests; stables and storehouses in the fields with no living quarters; a cistern, a water ditch, a cave, a wall and a dovecote in the field; and a house on a boat. None of these are included with the city.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives its second list: things that do NOT count as part of the city. The גמרא is quoting it because one item in this list will be used to try to answer the question from Step 11.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The common thread is that people do not live in these places, or they are not permanent buildings. Several items are named with the condition 'that has no בית דירה,' which tells us that if someone did live there, it would count. The first item, a נפש breached on two sides, is left with only two standing walls, so it connects directly to the איבעיא about two walls.

keyTerms.meaning: A monument or structure built over a grave
Living quarters, a place where a person lives
Are included in the city's extended boundary

steps.confusionAlert: Here נפש does NOT mean 'soul.' It means a stone monument built over a grave.

phrases.english: And these are not included with it (the city):
a grave-monument that was breached on two of its sides
phrases.notes: Two opposite walls are broken, so only two walls are left standing.

phrases.english: from here to there (straight through),

phrases.aramaic: וְהַגֶּשֶׁר וְהַקֶּבֶר שֶׁאֵין לָהֶן בֵּית דִּירָה,
phrases.english: and a bridge and a grave that have no living quarters,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת שֶׁאֵין לָהּ בֵּית דִּירָה לַחַזָּן,
phrases.english: and a synagogue that has no living quarters for the caretaker,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שֶׁאֵין לָהּ בֵּית דִּירָה לַכּוֹמָרִים,
phrases.english: and an idol temple that has no living quarters for the priests,
and the stables and storehouses in the fields
that have no living quarters,
and a cistern, a water ditch, and a cave
and a wall, and a dovecote that is in it (the field),
and the house on a boat
none of these are included with the city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא begun in Step 12 by giving its list of structures that are excluded.
steps.raayaObject: The איבעיא of whether two walls with a roof count as part of the city.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא listing structures that are not included in the city's boundaries.

steps.title: Proof from the breached monument: two walls with a roof do not count
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא focuses on the נפש breached on two sides. It suggests the monument still has a roof, which would prove that two walls with a roof do NOT count as part of the city.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, the ברייתא teaches: a grave-monument breached on two sides, from one side through to the other, is not included. Isn't this talking about a case where there is a roof? Then two walls with a roof do not count.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pulls out the one line of the ברייתא that matters and tries to use it to answer the איבעיא from Step 11.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A breached נפש is left with two standing walls. If we assume its roof is still in place, then this is exactly the case of two walls with a roof, and the ברייתא says it is not included. That would answer the איבעיא: such a structure does not count as part of the city.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case, it teaches (pointing to the relevant line)
Is it not? (introduces a suggested reading)

phrases.english: In any case, it teaches:
a grave-monument that was breached on two of its sides
from here to there.
Is it not talking about where there is a roof!
phrases.notes: If so, two walls with a roof are not included.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the specific inference from the ברייתא quoted in Step 13.
steps.raayaObject: Two walls with a roof are not included in the city.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא clause about a נפש breached on two sides, read as still having a roof.

steps.title: Rejection: the breached monument has no roof
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The ברייתא could be talking about a monument with no roof, so it tells us nothing about two walls WITH a roof.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It is talking about a case where there is no roof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own proof by reading the case differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the breached monument has no roof, it is just two bare walls. Of course that does not count, since even רב יהודה required three walls. So the ברייתא does not answer the איבעיא, and the question stays open.

phrases.english: No, it is where there is no roof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in Step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. It does not decide the איבעיא either way.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the breached monument still had a roof, but it can be read as having no roof at all.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא about a breached נפש does not settle whether two walls with a roof count, because that case may have no roof.

steps.title: What is a house on the sea used for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about the 'house on the sea' that the ברייתא counts as part of the city. What is such a house used for, that it should be included?
steps.simpleTranslation: A house on the sea: what is it good for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a different item in the ברייתא and asks a clarifying question about it. This sets up רב פפא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says this house IS included with the city. That only makes sense if it is a real, useful structure tied to the city. The גמרא wants to know what practical purpose it serves.

keyTerms.meaning: A house on (or by) the sea
What is it fit for? What is it used for?

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up two different items. בית שבים (a house on the sea) is in the list of structures that ARE included. בית שבספינה (a house on a boat) is in the list of structures that are NOT included. The גמרא is asking about the included one.

phrases.english: A house on the sea.
What is it fit for?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the איבעיא and clarifies another item in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical use a house on the sea has.

steps.title: רב פפא: a storage house for the ship's utensils
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that it is a structure used to unload and store the ship's equipment.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: it is a house made for clearing the ship's utensils into it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the question by naming a real use for the house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The house has a real, regular use: the ship's equipment is moved into it and stored there. Because it serves this ongoing purpose, the ברייתא counts it as part of the city.

keyTerms.meaning: To clear out or unload into

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
a house that is made for clearing into it
the utensils that are on the ship.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It is a storage house for the ship's equipment, and that use is why it counts as part of the city.

steps.title: Contradiction: רבי חייא says a cave is included
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא said a cave is not included, but רבי חייא taught that a cave is included.
steps.simpleTranslation: And is a cave not included with the city? But רבי חייא taught: a cave is included with the city!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's ruling on caves by quoting another source that says the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two teachings say opposite things about the same structure. Either one is wrong, or they must be talking about different kinds of caves.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't (he) teach? (introduces a contradicting source)

phrases.english: And is a cave not included with it?
But Rabbi Chiya taught:
A cave is included with it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a new difficulty on a different item of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a cave is not included in the city.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי חייא's ברייתא explicitly says a cave is included, which directly contradicts it.

steps.title: אביי: a cave counts when a building stands at its entrance
steps.stepSummary: אביי resolves the contradiction. רבי חייא is talking about a cave with a building at its opening, and the ברייתא is talking about a plain cave.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: רבי חייא means when there is a building at its entrance.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the contradiction by splitting it into two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plain cave is not a dwelling, so it does not count. When a building is built at its entrance, the whole thing is treated like a house near the city, so it does count. Both teachings are true, each for its own case.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the answer here

phrases.english: Abaye said:
When there is a building at its entrance.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי כְּשֶׁיֵּשׁ בִּנְיָן עַל פִּיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in Step 18.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two sources seem to disagree about every cave.
steps.terutzMaskana: A cave with a building at its entrance is included. A plain cave is not.
steps.whatToRemember: A cave on its own does not count as part of the city. Once a building stands at its entrance, it does.

steps.title: Why mention the cave if the building already counts?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אביי's answer: if there is a building at the cave's opening, the building alone should count, so the cave adds nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him get the rule because of the building itself!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on אביי's answer from the last step. If a building stands at the cave's opening, that building already counts as a house, so why talk about the cave at all?
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי said רבי חייא's cave counts because a building is at its opening. But a building counts toward the city all by itself. So it seems pointless for רבי חייא to mention the cave.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him derive it (from somewhere else) — why not get the rule from a simpler reason?

phrases.english: But let him derive it
phrases.notes: The גמרא is asking: why not just use a simpler reason?

phrases.english: because of the building itself!
phrases.notes: The building alone should be enough to count as a house.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's resolution in Step 19
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's explanation that רבי חייא means a cave with a building at its opening
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the building alone already counts as a house, mentioning the cave adds nothing, so רבי חייא's teaching would be pointless.

steps.title: The cave is needed to complete the minimum size
steps.stepSummary: The cave matters when the building is too small by itself. Building and cave together reach the minimum size of a house (4 by 4 אמות).
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where the cave serves to complete the building's size.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. רבי חייא's case is one where the building is too small to count alone, and the cave adds enough space to complete it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A structure must be at least 4 by 4 אמות to count as a house. Here the building alone falls short, but building plus cave reach the minimum together. So the cave really does matter, and רבי חייא's teaching is not pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a specific case)
To complete / fill out (the minimum size)

steps.whatToRemember: A plain cave does not count as part of the city. A cave with a building at its opening does count, and it matters when the cave helps the building reach the minimum size of a house.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary only
phrases.notes: The גמרא answers that this is needed only for one particular case.

phrases.english: to complete (the building's size).
phrases.notes: The cave plus building together reach 4 by 4 אמות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 20
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The building alone counts, so the cave seems unnecessary.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is a small building that only reaches house-size together with the cave, so the cave is essential.

steps.title: Hut-dwellers measure from their own doorways
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that people who live in flimsy huts are not treated as a city. Their תחום שבת is measured only from each person's own doorway.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: For those who live in huts, we measure only from the doorway of their homes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ruling from רב הונא. People living in flimsy huts do not get the 'city' treatment, so their 2,000 אמות start at their own doors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the discussion was about real cities, where the whole city counts as one unit and the תחום is measured from its edge. רב הונא says huts made of straw and branches do not join together into a city. So each hut-dweller measures from his own doorway.

keyTerms.meaning: People who live in huts (flimsy shelters of straw and branches)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a key question: what makes a group of dwellings count as a 'city' for תחום שבת? The rest of the sugya tests רב הונא's ruling.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
Those who dwell in huts,
phrases.notes: Flimsy shelters, not proper houses.

phrases.english: one does not measure for them
except from the entrance of their homes.
phrases.notes: The huts do not combine into a city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic about which kinds of dwellings count as a city
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hut-dwellers are not treated as a city; their תחום שבת is measured from each one's own doorway.

steps.title: The desert camp of tents was treated as one city
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא challenges רב הונא. The camp in the desert was huge, 3 by 3 פרסאות, and people walked to the back of it to relieve themselves, even on שבת. So a camp of tents was treated as one city.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא objected: The verse says 'They camped by the ירדן from בית הישימות.' רבה בר בר חנה said (in the name of רבי יוחנן): I saw that place myself, and it is three פרסאות by three פרסאות. And a ברייתא taught: When they went to relieve themselves, they did not go in front of the camp or to its sides, only behind it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא attacks רב הונא's ruling using the Jewish camp in the desert. He brings two facts: the camp was enormous, and people walked behind it to relieve themselves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The camp was 3 פרסאות long, about 12 מיל, which is far more than 2,000 אמות. People still walked all the way to the back of the camp, even on שבת. That only works if the whole camp counted as one city, yet it was made only of tents. So simple dwellings do seem to join into a city, which goes against רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: פרסאות — a measure of distance; one פרסה equals 4 מיל

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא never says 'this proves the camp was a city.' The question is implied. If people walked 12 מיל to the back of the camp on שבת, the whole camp must have counted as one city, even though it was only tents.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda raised an objection:
phrases.notes: An objection based on a source.

phrases.english: "And they camped by the Jordan
phrases.notes: במדבר 33:49

phrases.english: from Beit HaYeshimot",
phrases.notes: The verse continues: until אבל השטים.

phrases.english: and Rabba bar bar Chana said
(Rabbi Yochanan said):
phrases.notes: Bracketed attribution in the printed text.

phrases.english: I myself saw that place,
and it is three parasangs
phrases.notes: 3 פרסאות = 12 מיל

phrases.english: by three parasangs.
phrases.notes: Much bigger than 2,000 אמות.

phrases.english: And it was taught (in a baraita):
When they would relieve themselves —
they would not relieve themselves in front of them,
phrases.notes: Out of respect for the שכינה.

phrases.english: and not to their sides,
but only behind them?
phrases.notes: So people walked the full length of the camp, even on שבת. The camp must have counted as a city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's ruling in Step 22
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling that hut-dwellers do not form a city
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The desert camp was made only of tents and stretched 12 מיל, yet people walked to its back even on שבת. That means the tent camp counted as one city, which contradicts רב הונא.

steps.title: The desert camp was special because God fixed it
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers רב חסדא's challenge. The desert camp was treated as permanent because it camped and traveled by God's command. So it is no proof against רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: You are bringing a proof from the banners of the desert? About them it is written, 'By God's command they camped, and by God's command they traveled.' So it was as if their place was permanent.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends רב הונא. He shows that the desert camp is not a fair comparison to ordinary hut-dwellers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא argued that the tent camp in the desert counted as one city, so huts should count too. רבא says the desert camp was a unique case: God Himself set where they camped, which made it 'fixed' (קבוע). Ordinary huts have no such status, so רב הונא's rule still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: The tribal banners or formations of the Jewish camp in the desert
As if it were fixed or permanent
You are saying (here it means: you bring a proof from that?)

steps.whyThisMatters: A proof from a unique, miraculous situation does not prove anything about normal cases. The גמרא often pushes back on proofs this way.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
You are bringing a proof from the banners of the desert?
phrases.notes: This is a pushback question: that case is different.

phrases.english: Since it is written about them:
"By the command of God they camped,
phrases.notes: במדבר ט:כ

phrases.english: and by the command of God they traveled"
it is considered as though it were fixed (permanent) for them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: דִּגְלֵי מִדְבָּר קָאָמְרַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב חסדא's challenge from Step 23 and defends רב הונא's ruling from Step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the desert camp was a unique, divinely fixed situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The desert tent camp shows that any tent or hut settlement counts as one city.
steps.terutzMaskana: The desert camp counted as permanent only because God fixed its place. Ordinary huts do not count as a city, as רב הונא said.

steps.title: When a hut settlement becomes permanent
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי (quoted by רב חיננא בר רב כהנא) rules that if a hut settlement has three courtyards, each with two real houses, the whole settlement counts as fixed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חיננא בר רב כהנא said in the name of רב אשי: If there are three courtyards there, each with two houses, the settlement is considered fixed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a limit to רב הונא's rule. It explains when a hut settlement does count as a city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא said hut-dwellers are not a city. רב אשי adds a minimum: once there are three courtyards with two solid houses in each, the place is a real, permanent settlement. Then the תחום is measured from the edge of the whole settlement, not from each person's doorway.

keyTerms.meaning: They have become fixed or permanent

steps.whatToRemember: Huts alone are not a city (רב הונא). But if there are three courtyards with two real houses each, the settlement is fixed (רב אשי). The desert camp was fixed because of God's command (רבא).

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִינָּנָא בַּר רַב כָּהֲנָא
phrases.english: Rav Ḥinnana bar Rav Kahana said
that Rav Ashi said:
If there are three courtyards there
of two houses each —
they have become fixed (a permanent settlement).

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִינָּנָא בַּר רַב כָּהֲנָא אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב הונא's rule is defended, רב אשי adds the minimum needed for a hut settlement to count as permanent.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A settlement with three courtyards, each with two built houses, counts as a fixed settlement for measuring the תחום שבת.

steps.title: The hard life of hut-dwellers and desert travelers
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: people who live in huts and travel through deserts have very hard lives, and their wives and children are not truly 'theirs'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: People who live in huts and people who travel through deserts — their lives are not real lives, and their wives and children are not really their own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves הלכה and moves into an אגדה side-comment. The link is the topic of hut-dwellers (יושבי צריפין).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hut-dwellers, like shepherds, keep moving and stay in one place only briefly. Their lives are full of hardship, and they are often far from home and family. So their family life is unstable and unprotected, which is why their wives and children are 'not theirs'.

keyTerms.meaning: People who live in huts (temporary shelters)
Their lives are not lives (very hard lives)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new הלכה about תחומין. It is an אגדה side-comment linked only by the shared topic of hut-dwellers.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
Those who dwell in huts and those who travel through deserts —
their lives are not lives,
and their wives and children are not their own.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: יוֹשְׁבֵי צְרִיפִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from the הלכה status of hut-dwellers to an אגדה description of their way of life.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hut-dwellers and desert travelers live harsh, unstable lives, and their family life is not secure.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רב's harsh view of hut-dwellers
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא from אליעזר איש ביריא says the same idea even more strongly: hut-dwellers are like people who live in graves, and marrying their daughters is described with a verse of curse.
steps.simpleTranslation: This was also taught in a ברייתא. אליעזר איש ביריא says: People who live in huts are like people who live in graves. And about their daughters the verse says: 'Cursed is one who lies with any animal.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports רב's statement from the previous step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'תניא נמי הכי' means a ברייתא says the same thing. Comparing huts to graves shows how lifeless and cut off that life is. The verse of curse is a sharp rebuke of marrying their daughters. The גמרא gives the reason for this harsh view in the next steps (28–32).

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way (a ברייתא supports it)

steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה: huts alone do not make a city. The אגדה side-point: רב and the ברייתא both describe life in huts as harsh and unstable.

phrases.english: It was also taught this way (in a ברייתא):
Eliezer of Biriyya says:
Those who dwell in huts are like those who dwell in graves.
And about their daughters the verse says:
"Cursed is one who lies with any animal."
phrases.notes: דברים כז:כא. It's used here as a sharp scolding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב's aggadic statement in Step 26 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב's statement that hut-dwellers live harsh, unstable lives.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא quoting אליעזר איש ביריא, comparing hut-dwellers to grave-dwellers and applying a verse of curse to their daughters.

steps.title: Why are hut-dwellers described so harshly?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the harsh statement about hut-dwellers' wives and children.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב (Step 26) and the ברייתא (Step 27) said such harsh things about people who live in huts. This question sets up the answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps gave a strong statement but no reason for it. The גמרא now wants to know what about hut life causes the problem that their wives and children are not truly 'theirs.'

phrases.english: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: This refers to the statement that hut-dwellers' wives and children are not truly theirs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the statements in Steps 26-27.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason hut-dwellers' wives and children are described as not truly theirs.

steps.title: עולא: There are no bathhouses
steps.stepSummary: עולא explains that hut settlements have no bathhouses.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: Because they have no bathhouses.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא gives the first answer. Hut settlements have no bathhouses, so the men must travel far to bathe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While the husbands are away bathing, there is a concern that their wives may be unfaithful. That is why the children may not truly be the husband's. The problem comes from the men being away from home.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who often traveled between ארץ ישראל and בבל

phrases.english: Ulla said:
Because they have no bathhouses.
phrases.notes: So the men must go far away to bathe, leaving their wives alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first answer to the question in Step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Without bathhouses the men go far to bathe, and their wives are left alone.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: Everyone knows when the women immerse
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that in a small settlement, people know when a woman goes to immerse.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Because they notice one another's immersion.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a different answer. In such a small place, everyone knows when a woman goes out to the מקוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the women must walk far to immerse, an immoral man could follow a woman and take advantage of her being alone. For עולא the problem is the men being away. For רבי יוחנן the problem is the women being away and noticed.

keyTerms.meaning: A leading אמורא of ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Because they notice one another's immersion.
phrases.notes: Everyone knows when a woman goes far away to immerse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, competing answer to the question in Step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The women must go far to immerse, and in a small place everyone knows when, so a man could take advantage of them.

steps.title: What is the practical difference between the two reasons?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between עולא's reason and רבי יוחנן's reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether the two reasons would ever lead to a different result in real life. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both reasons reach the same conclusion that hut life is risky for marriages. The גמרא looks for a case where one reason applies and the other does not.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two answers given in Steps 29-30.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where עולא's reason and רבי יוחנן's reason would lead to different results.

steps.title: A river right next to the house
steps.stepSummary: The difference shows up when a river next to the house is fit for immersion but not for bathing.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a difference between them: a river that is close to the house.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a case where the two reasons split: a river right next to the house. The river is good for immersion but not for bathing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The women can immerse right near home, so רבי יוחנן's worry goes away. The men still have no bathhouse and must travel far to bathe, so עולא's worry is still there.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them
That is close to the house

steps.whatToRemember: עולא: the problem is that the men leave home to bathe. רבי יוחנן: the problem is that the women leave home to immerse. A river next to the house solves only רבי יוחנן's problem.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them:
a river that is close to the house.
phrases.notes: It is fit for immersion but not for bathing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 31 by giving the case where the two reasons split.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: With a river by the house, רבי יוחנן's concern is removed but עולא's concern remains.

steps.title: A תלמיד חכם should not live in a city without vegetables
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that a תלמיד חכם may not live in a city that has no vegetables.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: Any city that has no vegetables, a תלמיד חכם is not allowed to live there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new teaching about where a person should live. רב הונא says a תלמיד חכם should not live in a city without vegetables.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects to the earlier topic of places to live. רב הונא's point is about health: he assumes vegetables are good for a person, so a city without them is not a healthy place for a תלמיד חכם.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
Any city that has no vegetables —

phrases.aramaic: אֵין תַּלְמִיד חָכָם רַשַּׁאי לָדוּר בָּהּ.
phrases.english: a Torah scholar is not permitted to live there.
phrases.notes: This is for health reasons.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, related topic about places to live.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תלמיד חכם may not live in a city without vegetables.

steps.title: Challenge: A ברייתא says some foods are harmful
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether vegetables are really healthy, and begins quoting a ברייתא that lists three harmful things.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does that mean vegetables are good? But a ברייתא teaches: Three things increase waste, bend a person's posture, and take away one five-hundredth of a person's eyesight. And these are:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא. A ברייתא lists three things that harm the body. The list itself continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא assumed vegetables are healthy. The ברייתא is about to name things that weaken the body, and vegetables will apparently be among them. If so, this contradicts רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: But was it not taught in a ברייתא?

steps.confusionAlert: The list of the three things is cut off here and continues on the next amud. Do not look for it in this step.

phrases.english: Is that to say that vegetables are beneficial?
But was it not taught in a baraita:
Three things increase waste,
and bend one's posture,
and remove one five-hundredth
of the light of a person's eyes,
and these are:
phrases.notes: The list continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's assumption in Step 33 that vegetables are healthy.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's assumption that vegetables are beneficial.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא lists things that harm the body, apparently including vegetables. This contradicts the idea that a city needs vegetables for health.
